messages.text: I barely carried my feet between the desks, feeling the weight of every glance in the room. 'You looked like a deer caught in headlights up there. Don't worry, it gets easier.' Anna's voice pulled me back to the present, but I didn't know what to say, so I just nodded. She seemed satisfied and turned back toward Sensei Tanaka, who was already scribbling differential calculus on the blackboard. My mind was elsewhere, replaying the moment I had stepped through that doorway. I'd been the new kid before, but high school was a different world — a complex ecosystem of social hierarchies and unspoken rules I hadn't decoded yet.

I scanned the room, trying to memorize faces I'd forget by tomorrow. A bleached-haired boy slouched in the back corner, not paying attention. A group of girls near the window passed notes despite Sensei Tanaka's periodic glares. In the front row, a girl took notes with meticulous precision, her pen never pausing. And Anna kept glancing at me from the corner of her eye, as if she waited for something — as if she knew something I didn't.

The bell rang at noon, a shrill tone that shattered my fragile concentration. The classroom erupted into motion — chairs scraping, bags zipping, voices rising. I stayed seated, uncertain of where to go. The cafeteria was somewhere on the first floor, but the thought of navigating that crowded space alone made my stomach tighten. I felt invisible, a ghost among students who all seemed to know their place.
'Hey.' Anna's voice came from my left. She had turned in her chair and was facing me, chin resting on her crossed arms. 'You look lost.'

messages.name: I
messages.text: 'I'm fine,' I said, though my voice probably betrayed me.

messages.name: Anna
messages.text: 'Liar.' She smiled, and this time there was something genuine in it. 'Come on. I'll show you around. Consider it a welcome gift.'

Before I could refuse, she was already waiting by the doorway, relaxed and confident. With a reluctant sigh, I gathered my bag and followed her into the corridor. The hallway was a river of students, and Anna navigated it with ease. I trailed behind, trying not to bump into anyone, feeling awkward and out of place.

As we walked, I noticed Anna's presence created a ripple in the crowd. People nodded, whispered, glanced at me — the stranger following her like a lost puppy. 'You're popular,' I said, not meaning to say it out loud.

messages.name: Anna
messages.text: 'Something like that.' She glanced back, her expression unreadable.

We reached the cafeteria, which had large windows overlooking a small river. I could see the bank lined with willow trees, their branches dipping into the water. It was a peaceful sight, a stark contrast to the bustling room. Anna led me to a table near the window where two students were already seated: the meticulous note-taker from the front row and a boy with glasses I hadn't noticed before.
